title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
summary: Girl with a Pearl Earring is an oil painting by Dutch Golden Age painter Johannes Vermeer, dated c. 1665. Going by various names over the centuries, it acquired its present title towards the end of the 20th century. The work has been in the collection of the Mauritshuis in The Hague since 1902 and has been the subject of various literary and cinematic treatments.

sections.name: the girl
sections.description: She is shown in a three-quarter view against a dark background, looking over her shoulder with an enigmatic expression that often draws comparisons to the Mona Lisa.

sections.name: her eye
sections.description: Her wide, dark eye captures a glint of light, showing Vermeer's mastery of reflections and creating a sense of direct engagement with the viewer.

sections.name: her parted mouth
sections.description: Her lips are slightly parted as if she is about to speak, rendered with soft highlights that give them a moist, lifelike appearance.

sections.name: the pearl earring
sections.description: The focal point of the painting, the pearl is created with just a few strokes of white paint to represent reflected light, symbolizing purity or luxury.

sections.name: the turban
sections.description: The exotic headpiece uses ultramarine pigment, which was more expensive than gold at the time, indicating the subject is a 'tronie' rather than a standard portrait.

sections.name: the white collar
sections.description: The crisp white collar provides a sharp contrast against the dark background and the tan jacket, drawing the eye upward toward her face.

museum_facts: The Mauritshuis dates the painting to around 1665 and says it is on view in Room 15.
It is not a portrait of a known person but a “tronie,” a study of an imaginary figure in exotic dress.
Vermeer used soft transitions to model the girl’s face, while small dabs of paint suggest reflected light on her clothing.
The oversized pearl is probably an imitation: Vermeer suggested it with just two brushstrokes, and painted no silver hook.

guide_notes.the girl: This is her whole figure: a round head at the top with a few raised balls inside for her eye, nose and mouth, a straight line across the seventh row where her collar is, then her shoulders widening to the bottom edge. It looks like a portrait, but it is a tronie, a study of an imagined character, and no one knows who she was.
guide_notes.her eye: One eye fills the board: a wide almond outline, with a smaller ring inside on the left for her iris and a single raised ball in it for the pupil. A 2018 to 2020 study of the painting found tiny eyelashes around her eyes, too small to see without scanning.
guide_notes.her parted mouth: The top shape, peaking in the middle like a bow, is her upper lip; the empty row below it is the gap where her lips part, and the rounded bowl underneath is her lower lip. Her parted lips are part of why the painting is called the Mona Lisa of the North.
guide_notes.the pearl earring: The pearl is a teardrop outline, narrow at the top where it hangs and round at the bottom, with two short raised pairs inside: the bright highlight near the top and a soft glow near the bottom. Vermeer painted no hook joining it to her ear, only a few strokes of light, and it is far too big to be a real pearl.
guide_notes.the turban: The turban fills the board: a rounded outline that peaks at the top right, with a straight line across the fourth row where the blue band meets the yellow cloth piled above it, and the right edge running all the way down to the bottom where that cloth hangs. Its blue is natural ultramarine, ground from lapis lazuli brought from Afghanistan, one of the most expensive pigments of its time.
guide_notes.the white collar: A single curved line: it starts at the top right, sweeps down to the left edge in the middle, then curves back to the bottom right, like the letter C. That is the edge of her white collar, and the soft glow on the underside of the pearl is a reflection of it.
